title: Someone used Claude to build a chatbot that fits on a floppy disk
excerpt: A floppy disk sized chatbot that was trained on AI generated material can operate on DOS with 367K parameters.
content_html:
Published Nov 16, 2026, 6:56 AM EST

Hamed holds a B.A. in English Literature, and graduated top of his class. He loves music, tech gadgets, and exploring the latest in the world of LLMs. He also enjoys tinkering with creative software such as Logic Pro, Final Cut Pro, and Photoshop.

A lifelong musician, Hamed plays multiple instruments, including guitar, bass, and oud. He is equally fascinated by smart-home technology and can happily spend hours geeking out over connected lights, speakers, sensors, and automations that make everyday life a little more interesting. When he isn’t covering the latest tech news, he explores more creative topics on his Medium blog, works on his music, or clears his head by riding his motorcycle.

Summary

  • Tiny-2.1 is a Claude-built chatbot that fits on a floppy disk and runs on DOS with about 540 KB of free memory.
  • It can answer trivia and handle basic arithmetic, but the creator’s tests showed accuracy dropping from about 90% on familiar wording to 61% on unfamiliar questions.
  • Tiny-2.1 is a retrocomputing proof of concept. More capable small open-weight models can handle specific tasks like extracting details from notes or answering questions about an offline archive.

Open-weight LLMs are the latest buzz in tech nowadays, and not all workflows need the latest and greatest to get the job done — as the developer WollyMonjac has proved with Tiny-2.1, a chatbot built with Claude that runs on a Pentium or 486DX PC under DOS. The entire program and its model weights take up nothing more than half a megabyte combined, so you could technically fit both on a single floppy disk. To run it, you'll need about 540 KB of free conventional memory.

The developer used Claude's latest Fable 5.2 to write the transformer and Opus 5.5 to generate the training material. It covered about 3,500 facts and many examples of small talk and arithmetic. The model has 367,000 parameters, which is meager even compared to the lightweight Llama, whose parameter count sits at 3.21 billion.

What can a chatbot this small actually do?

Obviously, you should expect very little from Tiny 2.1, given its incredibly small size. Still, it can tell you the capital of Peru, spell "cat" backward, and solve some basic mathematical equations. You can phrase familiar questions a few different ways, and, even though it reads and writes one letter at a time, it can handle small typos. Moreover, the DOS interface even has a live display of the model's activity and makes robot noises through your speakers when it replies.

That said, it's not very difficult to push Tiny 2.1 to its limits. The creator says you'll get around 90% accuracy when asking questions phrased the way they were during training. However, accuracy dropped to 61% on test questions with new wording. Also, apparently division isn't really its thing, as it struggles to give you accurate answers. Tiny 2.1 does better with multiplication, though, so it's not entirely useless.

For hobbyists and testers, seeing how much Tiny gets right with so little memory is part of the fun, and the C source is on GitHub if you want to see how it works or tinker with it. But for everyday work, even if it's featherweight work, Tiny 2.1 struggles to be reliable. It's always fun to do these tests on different computers and see how they behave, as we did when we tried running local AI on a 10-year-old Celeron mini PC.

Smaller models can be enough

Though Tiny 2.1 is more of a proof of concept

WollyMonjac's creation is more of a proof of concept than a practical LLM to use for everyday work. Thankfully, there are many options between this half-a-megabyte model and the hefty ones that require a three-digit-GB RAM configuration. Hugging Face counted nearly 3 million public model repositories in its summer 2026 report, up from 2.43 million earlier in the year.

The important thing is to pick a job before you pick a model. We've reviewed some of the smallest local models available, and each comes with its own unique perks and advantages. Liquid AI's LFM3-1.7B, for instance, is a good lightweight model for extracting structured information from text. If your main task is pulling names and dates out of short notes, it can reliably fill those fields while running on your own hardware. We’ve also used Llama 3.2 3B Instruct on a low-powered home server to answer questions from downloaded reference material and archived forum posts.

Tiny 2.1 is a good excuse to dust off a DOS PC and see how far a few hundred kilobytes can take a chatbot over a weekend. It fails to be anything above and beyond a weekend DIY project, though.
